newsitem.title: CANADA: Queen Elizabeth set to tour still royalist Canada.
newsitem.headline: Queen Elizabeth set to tour still royalist Canada.

text.p: Five centuries after explorer John Cabot claimed Newfoundland for the English crown, the Canadian province is preparing for Queen Elizabeth's visit beginning on Monday with a celebration likely to warm any monarch's heart.
"The monarchy will never die in Newfoundland," said Ed Norsworthy, a fourth-generation Newfoundlander of English stock. "It's a big part of all of us, especially the older generation."

The queen is launching her Canadian tour with a three-day visit to Newfoundland to commemorate the 500th anniversary of Cabot's voyage to this rocky, windswept island in the north Atlantic. Newfoundland became Canada's 10th province in 1949.
The queen's Canadian visit - her 16th since becoming monarch in 1952 -- will also take her to Ontario before she leaves for home on July 2.

Fifty years after the independence of India -- the jewel in the crown -- and less than two weeks before the empire's last outpost, Hong Kong, is handed over to China, Britain's monarchy may not be as popular in the rest of Canada as in Newfoundland, but its symbols endure.

No republican movement has taken root here as it has in Australia. Queen Elizabeth remains Canada's head of state. She is represented by a governor general in Ottawa, a largely ceremonial post, and by lieutenant-governors in all 10 provinces.
She appears on Canadian coins and banknotes and the country still marks the birthday of her great great-grandmother Queen Victoria with a holiday.

Many towns and buildings are named after the royals. There is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary and the Queen Elizabeth Way -- the main highway from Toronto to the U.S. border -- and Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition in Canada's parliament, where members swear an oath of alliegance to the monarch.

"The queen represents traditions which are important, binding and quite popular," said Fred Langan, Canadian correspondent for London's Daily Telegraph, noting the "terrible fuss" in the 1960s when Canada replaced the red ensign with the maple leaf as its national flag.
"In many countries monarchies are still in vogue," said Langan. "That is clear from the 'bicycle monarchies' in the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark and Sweden."

While Queen Elizabeth copes with the sliding popularity of the royal family in Britain amid a seemingly endless soap opera of scandals surrounding her offspring and their spouses, her popularity in Canada appears intact.

That is not the case with others in her family. Canadians seemed bored with a visit by Prince Charles last year. An appearance by Prince Philip in Toronto at the Royal Winter Fair last autumn went largely unnoticed.
Yet even in French-speaking Quebec, where riots erupted during a royal visit in the 1960s, the British queen, who speaks flawless French, is regarded with polite interest.

"In Quebec she is perceived as a charming grandmother, but totally irrelevant, said Michel Vastel, a Montreal-based political columnist at Le Soleil newspaper in Quebec City. "The colonialists here are seen as the guys from Toronto, not from London."
